links.passage: This localized approach ensures that only a fraction of the soil surface is wetted, drastically reducing the volume of water available for soil evaporation (Al-agele, 2020).
supporting_passages: Drip irrigation, also termed micro-irrigation, represents the most significant departure from traditional methods by bypassing the field surface and the atmosphere as delivery mediums.
Water is delivered through a network of pipes and emitters directly to the plant's root zone at a low flow rate (Patel et al., 2023).
links.inference_note: The paragraph opens by naming drip irrigation and describing its root-zone delivery, and the cited sentence attributes the reduction of soil evaporation losses to this localized drip approach.
reference_entries: Al-agele, H. A. (2020). Irrigation Innovations to Increase Efficiency and Sustainability.

links.passage: Drip fertigation reduces nitrogen inputs by 7.2% and increases nitrogen productivity. Furthermore, drip irrigation can reduce nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions by up to 46% compared to sprinkler systems, which promote N2O flux through frequent wetting and drying cycles (ETH Zurich, 2021).
supporting_passages: Traditional systems have a high potential for nitrogen loss because they wet the entire soil surface.
links.inference_note: The preceding sentence frames the section around nitrogen loss from the soil, and the cited passage claims drip fertigation reduces nitrogen inputs and loss, which the paper treats as a nutrient-leaching (soil fertility) benefit.
